title: Economics & Trade

public.label: 01 / PUBLIC POLICY TRANSITION
public.title: Preparing an economy for life beyond trade preferences.
public.desc: LDC graduation alters preference margins, financing conditions and the terms of competition. Research helps sequence a transition rather than react to each shock separately.
public.ref: Synthetic teaching scenario. No client result is asserted.
problems: Fragmented intelligence on preferences and access
Gaps in productive capacity and export diversification

private.label: 01 / EXPORTER MARKET-ACCESS STRATEGY
private.title: What does the loss of a tariff preference mean for an exporter?
private.desc: When preferential access changes, the immediate impact depends on buyers, margins, country of origin, product mix and substitution possibilities—not a headline tariff alone.
private.ref: Synthetic teaching scenario. No client result is asserted.
private.problemTitle: A buyer strategy built on one advantage.
problems: Price competitiveness tied to preferences
Country and buyer concentration poorly mapped
Limited analysis of switching and certification costs
outputs: Buyer- and product-level tariff exposure map

public.label: 02 / TRADE POLICY AND TARIFF SHOCKS
public.title: Turning tariff uncertainty into a policy response.

public.ref: Synthetic teaching scenario. No client result is asserted.
public.problemTitle: A single shock. Many competing claims.
problems: Tariff headlines mistaken for predicted export losses
Product exposure and elasticities not reconciled

private.label: 02 / EXPORT PRICE AND DEMAND RISK
private.title: Protecting margins when foreign market conditions turn.
private.desc: An exporting firm may face higher buyer prices, weaker orders and fluctuating exchange rates at the same time. A useful strategy separates price, volume, margin and local-currency cash flow.
private.ref: Synthetic teaching scenario. No client result is asserted.
private.problemTitle: Commercial decisions made from headlines.
problems: FX revenue confused with real profitability
Buyer price sensitivity untested

public.label: 03 / TRADE IN SERVICES
public.title: Making invisible trade barriers visible.

Regulatory and payments constraints unmapped

methodReferences.label: WITS SMART theoretical framework
methodReferences.author: World Bank
methodReferences.role: Partial-equilibrium modelling context; this lab is not SMART and does not calibrate its 60% pass-through from this reference

method: Constant-elasticity demand with an assumed 60% exchange-rate pass-through. All indices use a baseline of 100. Positive FX change means depreciation: more local currency per US dollar.
formula: Producer price = 1 − 0.6d/(1+d); buyer price = (1+t) × producer price; quantity = buyer price^(−ε); USD receipts = producer price × quantity; local receipts = USD receipts × (1+d).
limits: The 60% coefficient is synthetic. There is no supply response, competitor response, capacity constraint or fitted trade dataset. These are scenario indices, not an official forecast.

guidance.question: How sensitive are export volumes and receipts to tariffs, exchange rates and demand elasticity?
guidance.assumption: Baseline indices are 100. FX pass-through is assumed to be 60%; elasticity is selected, not estimated.
guidance.rule: Compare each index with 100 and test the direction of change. An index below 100 is a modelled decline, not evidence of a welfare loss of the same size.
guidance.next: Obtain product–destination tariffs, transaction prices, volumes, capacity and competitor data; estimate elasticities and pass-through before advising on policy.
guidance.chart: Horizontal: additional tariff (%). Vertical: export volume index (baseline 100). The table also reports buyer price and receipts indices. The selected dot is the current tariff.
guidance.risk: Partial-equilibrium sensitivity only; no welfare, employment or general-equilibrium estimate.
guidance.parameterOrigin: Original teaching prototype; no fitted trade observations supplied.

methodReferences.label: Guidelines for the Economic Analysis of Projects
methodReferences.author: Asian Development Bank
methodReferences.role: Economic-appraisal methods; this lab does not implement the full framework or calibrate parameters from it

method: An initial Year 0 investment followed by equal annual net flows. Benefits fall and operating costs rise under the selected stress assumption. NPV includes Year 0; IRR is the discount rate at which NPV is zero.
formula: Annual net flow = benefit × (1 − stress) − operating cost × (1 + stress/2). NPV = −investment + Σ(net flow/(1+r)^year). IRR solves NPV = 0 for this conventional cash-flow pattern.
limits: Synthetic flows exclude residual value, taxes, replacement costs, inflation, financing and shadow-price adjustments. Public/private context does not by itself establish ENPV/FNPV or EIRR/FIRR. Generic NPV and IRR describe only the entered demonstration flows.

guidance.question: Under which cash-flow and discount assumptions does an illustrative investment have positive NPV?
guidance.assumption: Year 0 investment, equal annual flows, end-of-year discounting and no residual value. Case selection changes these synthetic flows.
guidance.rule: NPV = 0 is the arithmetic threshold at the selected discount rate. A positive NPV here is insufficient for an investment recommendation or a public economic appraisal.
guidance.next: Obtain dated investment, operating, replacement and residual flows; specify currency and price basis, taxes, externalities, shadow prices and financing separately.
guidance.chart: Horizontal: year, including Year 0. Vertical: discounted net flow in USD millions. Bars below zero are outflows; the full table uses the same annual values.
guidance.risk: This single teaching account is neither an independently prepared economic account nor an investor financing model. No ENPV/EIRR or FNPV/FIRR conclusion is asserted.
guidance.parameterOrigin: Case-specific investment, benefit, operating cost, years and default discount rate from the original prototype; no underlying project accounts supplied.

methodReferences.label: Principles of Accounting, Volume 2: Managerial Accounting, section 3.1
methodReferences.author: Franklin, Graybeal and Cooper; OpenStax
methodReferences.role: Contribution-margin and cost-volume-profit methods; no calibration of the synthetic firm or demand elasticity

method: A stylised monthly enterprise with 1,200 units of demand at a price of $120, fixed costs of $29,000, constant demand elasticity and productivity reducing variable unit cost.
formula: Units = 1200 × (price/120)^(−elasticity); effective cost = variable cost/(1+productivity); profit = units × (price−effective cost) − 29000; break-even units = ceil(29000/contribution) when contribution > 0.
limits: Demand and cost assumptions are synthetic. No taxes, credit, competitors or capacity constraints are modelled. Nonpositive unit contribution means break-even is unattainable under these assumptions.

guidance.question: What volume covers fixed costs at the selected price and effective variable cost?
guidance.assumption: Monthly fixed cost is $29,000; demand is 1,200 units at $120 before the selected elasticity adjustment. Productivity reduces variable cost only.
guidance.rule: Operating profit crosses zero at fixed cost divided by positive unit contribution. Displayed break-even rounds up to a whole unit. With contribution ≤ 0 there is no finite break-even.
guidance.next: Validate transaction-level demand, capacity, variable and fixed costs, seasonality and competitor responses; investigate whether demand at the proposed price is attainable.
guidance.chart: Horizontal: units per month. Vertical: operating profit in USD per month. Solid line: profit at fixed selected price/cost; dot: demand implied by the elasticity model; dashed marker: break-even if in range.
guidance.risk: The volume sweep holds price and effective unit cost fixed; it is not a second demand curve or a forecast of sales.
guidance.parameterOrigin: Original stylised enterprise assumptions; no company observations supplied.

methodReferences.label: Impact Evaluation in Practice, second edition
methodReferences.author: Gertler, Martinez, Premand, Rawlings and Vermeersch; World Bank and Inter-American Development Bank
methodReferences.role: Evaluation and identification methods; not the source of the four synthetic percentages

method: Two groups observed before and after an intervention. The arithmetic compares their changes, measured in percentage points (pp). Causal interpretation requires credible identification, including parallel trends.
formula: Treated change = treated endline − baseline; comparison change = comparison endline − baseline; DiD = treated change − comparison change; counterfactual = treated baseline + comparison change.
limits: There are no observations, uncertainty intervals or parallel-trend diagnostics. Arithmetic alone establishes no causal effect. Extreme inputs can produce an infeasible counterfactual outside 0–100%; the chart displays and flags that result without silently clipping it.

guidance.question: How does the treated group’s before–after change compare with the comparison group’s change?
guidance.assumption: Four synthetic outcome percentages and one constructed counterfactual. There is no sample, standard error or confidence interval.
guidance.rule: A zero DiD contrast means equal changes in this illustration. A nonzero contrast alone establishes no causal effect. Counterfactuals outside 0–100% flag infeasible percentage assumptions.
guidance.next: Check pre-intervention trends, group composition, treatment timing, spillovers, concurrent shocks, attrition and missingness; then specify an identification and inference strategy.
guidance.chart: Horizontal: before and after. Vertical: outcome (%). Solid: treated; dashed: comparison; dotted: constructed treated counterfactual. Differences are percentage points, not percentage changes.
guidance.risk: Identification checklist: parallel trends, stable composition, timing, no spillovers and attrition — all Not assessed. These inputs cannot supply those diagnostics.
guidance.parameterOrigin: Four synthetic percentages entered by the reader; no participant-level observations supplied.

methodReferences.label: The Green Book
methodReferences.author: HM Treasury
methodReferences.role: Appraisal and opportunity-cost context; no evidence for the synthetic time coefficients or BDT 650/hour assumption

method: The baseline is 1.5 core hours plus 24% rework at 2.2 hours per instance. Up to five of ten assumed steps can be removed. Digital uptake and simplification affect core time; rework is modelled separately.
formula: Baseline = 1.5 + 0.24 × 2.2 hours; new core = 1.5 × (1−0.065 × steps) × (1−0.36 × digital uptake); new total = core + rework × 2.2; annual hours released = (baseline−new total) × monthly cases × 12.
limits: All coefficients and the BDT 650/hour valuation are synthetic. Time opportunity value is not a cash saving or budget reduction. Negative released hours mean workload increased.

guidance.question: How might simplification, digital uptake and rework change administrative effort?
guidance.assumption: Baseline: 1.5 core hours + 0.24 × 2.2 rework hours per case. Digital and step coefficients, monthly volume and BDT 650/hour are synthetic.
guidance.rule: Zero annual hours released means no workload change. Negative values mean extra workload. Staff-time opportunity value does not establish a budget saving or fiscal space.
guidance.next: Collect time-and-motion observations, demand volumes, channel uptake, rework reasons, implementation costs and service-quality/distributional measures.
guidance.chart: Horizontal: staff hours per case, common zero and scale. Rows: before and after. Core handling is solid; rework is hatched. Component totals match the table.
guidance.risk: Released capacity requires an operational plan; service quality, access, transition costs and actual cash expenditure are outside the model.

methodReferences.author: Government Project Delivery and Cabinet Office
methodReferences.role: Project-delivery governance and planning context; no calibration of linear package throughput or probability of completion

method: A linear throughput illustration with 120 equivalent work packages, 0.75 packages/person/week and an illustrative 24-week target. The fixed comparison uses 10 people, 65% availability, 24% rework and 23% dependency drag.
formula: Weekly rate = team × 0.75 × availability × (1−dependency drag)/(1+rework); duration = ceil(120/rate); schedule gap = 24−duration.
limits: This is not a critical-path or resource-loaded schedule. It has no real dependencies, holidays, cost model or uncertainty distribution. The chart horizon expands to include slow scenarios.

guidance.question: How do availability, rework and dependency drag change illustrative throughput and completion time?
guidance.assumption: 120 equivalent packages; 0.75 packages/person/week; fixed baseline of 10 people, 65% availability, 24% rework and 23% dependency drag.
guidance.rule: Completion within 24 weeks meets the illustrative target. Duration is rounded up to whole weeks; the chart shows continuous throughput capped at 120 packages.
guidance.next: Build a resource-loaded schedule with actual package sizes, dependency logic, calendars, skills, costs and uncertainty; test against delivery records.
guidance.chart: Horizontal: weeks, expanding for slow scenarios. Vertical: cumulative completed packages. Dashed: fixed baseline; solid: selected scenario; vertical dotted marker: week 24.
guidance.risk: Dependency drag is a scalar assumption, not a dependency network. This does not perform critical-path analysis or estimate a completion probability.
guidance.parameterOrigin: Original linear teaching model; no observed task-level delivery dataset supplied.
